title: Data breaches are coming fast and furious. Are businesses doing enough to protect your data?
summary: Recent data breaches at Bell and Staples are the latest in a swath of incidents where consumers' personal data was accessed by bad actors. As AI tools make it easier to carry out hacks, many…

image.caption: As AI makes cyber incidents more likely, experts say some businesses are taking the threat seriously, but many are still leaving their customers' personal data exposed. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: First it was a data breach at Staples, with the company alerting staplesprint.ca customers Friday that some personal information was accessed in a recent security incident.

Then came a notice from Bell, saying an "agentic threat actor" had accessed personal information like names, phone numbers and email addresses, impacting customers of Bell, Bell Aliant, Bell MTS, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile. Agentic usually refers to AI tools that can act independently.

The incidents are just the latest examples of breaches — Loblaws, Save-on-Foods, Montreal car-sharing company Communauto and telecomm provider Eastlink have all made headlines for data incidents in the past few months.
For Bell customers like Anna Stephenson, who received an email this week saying her data might have been compromised, news of another hack doesn't feel all that surprising anymore.
"It's kind of the world we live in now where we have to sort of deal with these things," she said.

blocks.text: Though she understands Bell's challenge in staying one step ahead of criminals, Stephenson wants to see companies do more to protect the valuable data they keep about customers.
"In my opinion, companies need to invest more in that security, and hopefully that's something that Bell's looking into," Stephenson said.
Bell cyberattack raises fear AI is making data breaches easier

The experts agree. As AI tools make it easier to carry out hacks, lots of businesses are trying to keep up with the onslaught of attacks — but security and data experts say poor data management and security practices often leave consumer information more vulnerable than it should be.

Too much data, not enough protection

Canadian privacy laws require companies to follow 10 principles when collecting, using and safeguarding personal information. When a breach happens that creates a real risk of harm, businesses have to report it to the privacy commissioner, notify individuals as soon as possible and keep records about the breach.
Those rules put the onus on businesses to manage and protect consumer data, according to Sharon Bauer, a lawyer and founder of Bamboo Data Consulting.

blocks.text: "It is their responsibility to make sure that the data is secure," said Bauer.

While federal courts can fine businesses up to $100,000 if they fail to take certain steps, like report a breach, the federal privacy commissioner can't hand out fines itself. Bauer says that means the existing rules don't always have enough teeth to make companies feel like they need to comply.

Sharon Bauer is a Toronto-based privacy lawyer and founder of Bamboo Data Consulting. Often, businesses are keeping too much customer data they don't need, making it vulnerable to potential breaches, Bauer says. (Submitted by Sharon Bauer)
And best practices for keeping data aren't always followed. While lots of businesses have to keep some personal info on file, Bauer says many keep too much information that they simply don't need.
"It's probably one of the biggest risks that we find in almost every company that we work with," Bauer said.

She says companies might keep dates of birth that aren't being used, for example. Not storing data is the best way to prevent it from being stolen, according to Bauer, so keeping old or out of date customer information creates an unnecessary risk.

Terry Cutler, CEO of Cyology Labs, which provides cybersecurity services to small and medium-sized businesses, says many companies are often simply unaware of how vulnerable they are. He says some businesses he's worked with will use software that keeps part of their systems safe, thinking it covers their bases, while other parts of their network are exposed.

Cutler says a lot of companies currently "don't have the proper detection technology to know there's a hacker in their system, and they don't have a good response plan to get the hacker out once he's been detected."
And with AI making it easier for hackers to steal valuable data, the importance of taking cyber issues seriously is growing, too.

blocks.text: Brent Arnold, founder of cybersecurity and privacy law firm Capstan Legal, says hackers can essentially automate attacks using AI, as agentic tools can work on their own to solve a problem once they're given an end goal — like hacking into software.
He says he's seen a deluge of attacks by hackers moving at hyper speed in recent months, something likely being driven by AI.
"It all happens a lot faster before it can be detected," he said.
One in four malicious data breaches are now powered by AI, according to IBM's 2026 data breach report — a 56 per cent increase compared to the year before.
Arnold points out that the standard for protecting data isn't perfection, but that companies should take reasonable steps to prevent data theft.
Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database
However, as threats become more sophisticated, he says businesses will need to raise their prevention measures to match.
"The standard is always reasonable measures, but what that looks like is getting more and more sophisticated as the attacks get more and more sophisticated."
Some firms stepping up
While some companies might not be keeping up with cyber risks, Bob Gordon, strategy advisor for the Canadian Cyber Threat Exchange, says others are taking the issue very seriously.

The cyber exchange is made up of big and small businesses that share information about cyber threats, including how hackers might attack and what evidence they may leave. Sharing this intelligence is a big help to smaller companies, Gordon says, because they often have fewer resources to pour into security.

Gordon says the exchange has attracted new members in recent months. He says it's a sign that businesses are starting to realize cyber security isn't just a tech concern, but rather a major risk that can impact consumer trust or even temporarily shut down operations in a worst-case scenario.
Cutler says calls to his cybersecurity firm are up by about 40 per cent — mostly from companies wanting to know how hackable they are and how they can prevent breaches.
Communauto was hit by a data breach — here’s what you need to know
Some companies have also stepped up prevention measures after breaches.

Communauto, for example, experienced a security incident earlier this year when it said an employee accessed customers' personal information. While a spokesperson said in an email that there's no evidence the stolen data was leaked, the company is still monitoring the dark web for it. Certain personal information will now be deleted or anonymized sooner, and access to customer data is now further restricted internally, the spokesperson said.
After its breach, Bell said it was investigating and had reached out to the RCMP's cyber crime unit. Staples said it was taking its breach "very seriously," and had also launched an investigation.
Cracking down with new rules
On top of those efforts, a new federal bill making its way through Parliament could bring tougher privacy rules.

Bill C-36 isn't yet law, but it would introduce stricter requirements about deleting customer data after it's been used — or whenever a person requests deletion — more measures about how it's stored and the ability to impose major fines in the millions of dollars if organizations don't follow the rules.

Arnold says he's not sure stronger laws will have much impact.
"The big problem is, companies often just don't even think about this," he said.

If the issue isn't on their radar, the threat of greater fines won't move the needle according to Arnold, meaning education about some of the free or cheap resources available to businesses could be a better place to start.

blocks.text: While Bauer says the new rules might not be perfect, they would up the ante for businesses to comply.
"I think that this is a wake up call for all businesses to start to think about how they handle … personal information and how they protect it."
